info.name: Parity Classify Sandbox
info.description:
Try the Parity Classify Sandbox API — a single endpoint (POST /v1/classify) that takes one bank transaction and returns its classified role (e.g. payroll, revenue, transfer) plus a plain-language reason.

Before you start:
1. Select the "Parity Sandbox" environment (top right).
2. Get a sandbox API key from the Parity team and paste it into that environment's `sandbox_api_key` variable (leave it blank and every request here will 401 — see the "Invalid API key" example to see what that looks like on purpose).
3. Run any request under "Example Transactions" to see a live classification.

Each saved request below is a different kind of transaction, chosen to show the real range of what this endpoint returns — not just one happy path.

item.name: Example Transactions
item.description: Three real transaction shapes sent to the same POST /v1/classify endpoint: an obvious payroll payment, an obvious revenue deposit, and a deliberately ambiguous one where the classifier's reasoning is worth reading closely.

request.description: A large, round, outbound payment described as a payroll run — the clearest possible payroll case. `signed_amount_cents` is negative because money is leaving the account. Expect the response's `role` to come back as payroll with a reason that references the descriptor and the outbound direction.
An inbound payout from a payment processor — the clearest possible revenue case. `signed_amount_cents` is positive because money is arriving. Expect `role` to come back as revenue.

An inter-account transfer flagged with `is_transfer: true` but described generically ("operating account", not a named counterparty). This is the interesting one to run: it shows how the classifier handles a transaction that isn't obviously payroll or revenue. Read the `classification_reason` in the response closely — it's the whole point of this example.

Same endpoint, same request shape as the examples above, but with a deliberately bad `x-api-key` (hardcoded here, not the environment variable, so this fails even after you've set a real key). This shows the real 401 behavior a partner sees when their key is missing, wrong, or not yet issued — a clean `{"detail": "Invalid API key"}`, no stack trace or server detail leaked.
